Prepare your own data

prepare-your-data.Rmd

Use this page when adapting MicroFun to your own study. If you want to try the published example first, start with Study data and downloads, then follow Standard or Stratified.

The shared workflow supports Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species when annotations are available. The demonstration uses Genus; the downloaded Species column is empty, so its deepest usable rank is Genus. Keep the original ASV-level object and change rank before refitting.

Choose the PICRUSt2 output

A standard table pools predicted contributions within each sample. A stratified table keeps the ASV–function–sample links needed for contributor analysis.

Your question Required input Continue with
Which community functions differ between groups? Unstratified feature-by-sample matrix and sample metadata Standard study
Which functions differ within a taxon, or which taxa contribute differently to a function? Stratified contributions and ASV-level phyloseq object, with a matching tree for phylogeny views Stratified study

Generate PICRUSt2 output

Start with representative ASV sequences and a matching feature table. The sequence identifiers must agree with the feature-table rows. For PICRUSt2 installation and full options, use the official documentation.

picrust2_pipeline.py \
  -s dna-sequences.fasta \
  -i feature-table.biom \
  -o picrust2_out \
  -p 8

Add --stratified when you need contributor tables. Retain the ASV taxonomy, sample metadata and phylogenetic tree from your sequence analysis alongside these outputs.

Typical community-level files include KO_metagenome_out/pred_metagenome_unstrat.tsv, EC_metagenome_out/pred_metagenome_unstrat.tsv and pathways_out/path_abun_unstrat.tsv. The first column holds feature IDs and the remaining columns hold sample abundances. Contribution tables are long tables, typically named pred_metagenome_contrib.tsv.gz.

Check a community-level table

Read your KO file and metadata, then select the same samples in both. Replace these paths and group names with your own. Keep feature IDs as matrix row names.

library(MicroFun)

meta <- read.delim("my_study/metadata.tsv", check.names = FALSE)
ko_table <- read.delim(
  "picrust2_out/KO_metagenome_out/pred_metagenome_unstrat.tsv",
  check.names = FALSE
)
ko_table[[1]] <- sub("^ko:", "", ko_table[[1]], ignore.case = TRUE)
reference <- "Control"
target <- "Treatment"
meta <- meta[meta$group %in% c(reference, target), , drop = FALSE]
meta$group <- factor(meta$group, levels = c(reference, target))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(meta$sample_name),
          !anyDuplicated(ko_table[[1]]),
          all(meta$sample_name %in% names(ko_table)[-1]),
          all(table(meta$group) > 0))
ko_abundance <- as.matrix(ko_table[, meta$sample_name, drop = FALSE])
rownames(ko_abundance) <- ko_table[[1]]
stopifnot(is.numeric(ko_abundance), all(is.finite(ko_abundance)),
          all(ko_abundance >= 0))
ko_table <- data.frame(
  function_id = rownames(ko_abundance),
  as.data.frame(ko_abundance, check.names = FALSE), check.names = FALSE
)
kegg_abundance <- ko2kegg_abundance(data = ko_table)

Continue from Fit and annotate the comparison using these objects and your own output directory. Replace the demonstration feature lists with IDs from your study when making selected-feature plots.

The conversion uses a bundled local KO-to-KEGG membership map. Online pathway annotation is a separate operation. See mapping and network access before changing reference inputs.

Keep the links intact

The contribution table tells us which ASV contributes to which function in each sample. The phyloseq object supplies the corresponding taxonomy and sample groups. If those identifiers do not match, the analysis cannot reliably connect a contribution to its taxon or cohort.

Keep the ASV identifiers until MicroFun performs the requested aggregation. Aggregating the phyloseq object to the analysis rank first can remove the identifiers needed to match the original contribution table and tree tips.

Prepare the stratified inputs

Table 1. Stratified inputs
Input What MicroFun expects
PICRUSt2 contribution table A tab-delimited long table, optionally gzipped, with sample, taxon, function, and taxon_function_abun. Typical filenames include pred_metagenome_contrib.tsv.gz and KO_contrib.tsv.gz.
ASV-level phyloseq object ASV identifiers in its taxonomy rows, a populated column for the chosen rank, and a metadata column for the comparison. Keep ASV identifiers until MicroFun aggregates them.
Optional phylogenetic tree ASV tip labels matching the taxonomy row names. A tree in phyloseq or an explicit Newick file can be used.

The taxon column contains ASV IDs. The function column contains IDs in the selected namespace, such as K00844 for KO. Use raw predicted taxon_function_abun for KO-to-KEGG and direct KEGG runs. Some other modes accept norm_taxon_function_contrib with a compatible backend. Keep contributions finite and nonnegative.

library(phyloseq)

strat_path <- "my_study/KO_contrib.tsv.gz"
ps <- readRDS("my_study/phyloseq_asv.rds")
group_col <- "group"
rank <- "Genus"
reference <- "Control"
target <- "Treatment"

# For an .RData file containing an object named ps, use this load pattern.
# input <- new.env()
# load("my_study/phyloseq_asv.RData", envir = input)
# ps <- input$ps

# If needed, subset the cohort before the checks below.
# ps <- prune_samples(sample_data(ps)$Cohort == "Cohort_A", ps)
# ps <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps) > 0, ps)

stopifnot(file.exists(strat_path), inherits(ps, "phyloseq"))
meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))
taxonomy <- as(tax_table(ps), "matrix")
stopifnot(group_col %in% names(meta), rank %in% colnames(taxonomy))

selected <- rownames(meta)[meta[[group_col]] %in% c(reference, target)]
ps <- prune_samples(selected, ps)
meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))
group_counts <- table(factor(meta[[group_col]], levels = c(reference, target)))
print(group_counts)
stopifnot(all(group_counts > 0), sum(group_counts) > 5L)

ids <- data.table::fread(strat_path, select = c("sample", "taxon"),
                         colClasses = "character", showProgress = FALSE)
missing_samples <- setdiff(sample_names(ps), ids$sample)
selected_asvs <- unique(ids$taxon[ids$sample %in% sample_names(ps)])
matched_asvs <- intersect(taxa_names(ps), selected_asvs)
print(c(missing_samples = length(missing_samples),
        matched_asvs = length(matched_asvs),
        contribution_asvs = length(selected_asvs)))
stopifnot(length(missing_samples) == 0L, length(matched_asvs) > 0L)
rm(ids)

Review the overlap before fitting. If IDs use different prefixes or representations, reconcile them from a verified sample or ASV mapping. Extra samples in a contribution file can remain when you analyze a phyloseq subset. Every selected sample must appear somewhere in the file. The default min_samples = 5 requires more than five eligible samples in a table, with at least two groups represented.

Continue with your own inputs

Reuse the preparation logic in the Stratified study, replacing its study-loading lines with the checked ps, strat_path, rank and contrast above. Replace keep_genera and keep_kos with selections suited to your project. The remaining preparation creates ps_taxa, taxa_strat_path and fun_strat_path before either analysis is fitted. For a rank other than Genus, the demonstrated preparation uses all assigned taxa at that rank.

Fit the taxon-centered direction first. The optional function-centered route uses the full ps and only the selected functions. Always select functions before fitting and plotting; analyzing an entire function library can take substantially longer. Keep the original ASV tree in ps for phylogeny views.

Use Differential analysis options to choose a method suited to your data and design. After fitting, use Visualization guides for figure selection, parameters and export. These guides work with your fitted study objects as well as the demonstration results.
